front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidises an alkene to form a diol without fully breaking the C=C bond.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> is a mild oxidising agent. It oxidises the alkene so that both carbons of the double bond gain an -OH group, forming a diol.

Butan-2-ol gives a positive iodoform test because it can be oxidised to a methyl ketone.

front_blocks.md: Why does a tertiary alcohol not change the colour of acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>?

back_blocks.md: A **tertiary alcohol** cannot be oxidised because the carbon bearing the -OH group has **no hydrogen atom** attached to it. Without a C-H bond at that carbon, oxidation cannot occur, so the orange colour of Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> is **unchanged**.

front_blocks.md: Are alcohols stronger or weaker acids than water? Give a reason.

back_blocks.md: Alcohols are **weaker** acids than water. The alkyl group in the alkoxide ion donates electron density to the oxygen, making it more likely to re-accept a proton and reform the alcohol, so [H<sup>+</sup>(aq)] is lower than in water.

Alcohols dissociate to a greater extent than water when dissolved in solution.

Alcohols have a low degree of dissociation. The equilibrium ROH ⇌ RO<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> lies far to the left, giving a lower [H<sup>+</sup>] than water.

front_blocks.md: Why does the alkoxide ion (RO<sup>-</sup>) tend to re-accept a proton more readily than the hydroxide ion (OH<sup>-</sup>)?

back_blocks.md: The alkoxide ion has an **electron-donating alkyl group** attached to the oxygen. This increases **electron density** on the O<sup>-</sup> atom, making it more likely to attract and accept a proton. The hydroxide ion has no such alkyl group, so its oxygen is less electron-rich.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The longer the hydrocarbon chain in an alcohol, the stronger the positive inductive effect and the weaker the acid.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

Longer alkyl chains have a greater positive inductive effect, donating more electron density to the O<sup>-</sup> atom of the alkoxide ion, increasing its tendency to re-accept a proton and reducing the acidity further.

front_blocks.md: What happens to the position of the equilibrium when water dissociates compared to when an alcohol dissociates?

back_blocks.md: In both cases the equilibrium lies to the left, but water **dissociates to a greater extent** than alcohols. Water therefore produces a **higher [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**(aq)]**, making it a **stronger acid** than alcohols.
